Adam Smith: Adam Smith was born in 1723 in Kirkcaldy, a small port town in Fife, Scotland. He studied at the University of Glasgow and at Balliol College, Oxford. After giving public lectures in Edinburgh, he became professor of logic and later of moral philosophy at Glasgow. In the 1760s he toured France as tutor to the young Duke of Buccleuch, meeting leading French thinkers. He spent his last years as a commissioner of customs in Edinburgh, where he died in 1790.

Smith published The Theory of Moral Sentiments in 1759, exploring how sympathy and the judgment of an imagined impartial spectator shape our moral lives. An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations followed in 1776, analysing the division of labour, markets, free trade and the proper role of government. Read together, his two great books reveal a thinker as concerned with ethics as with wealth, which is why economists, philosophers and historians still return to him.
Aesop: Almost nothing about Aesop can be confirmed. Ancient tradition, reported by Herodotus, describes him as a slave on the island of Samos in the sixth century BC, and later writers claimed he won his freedom and died at Delphi. A fictional Life of Aesop, written centuries later, made him a clever slave who outwits his masters. Some scholars doubt he existed at all.

The fables credited to Aesop are short tales, usually featuring animals who talk and behave like people, each ending with a practical lesson. The Tortoise and the Hare, The Fox and the Grapes, The Boy Who Cried Wolf and The Ant and the Grasshopper are among the most familiar. Passed on by word of mouth, they were later retold in verse by Phaedrus and Babrius, and much later by Jean de La Fontaine. Their brevity, humour and clear morals have kept them at the heart of childhood reading for more than two thousand years.
Alessandro Manzoni: Alessandro Manzoni was born in Milan in 1785. His mother was the daughter of the Enlightenment jurist Cesare Beccaria, and as a young man he lived with her in Paris among liberal intellectuals. After his marriage to Enrichetta Blondel he returned to the Catholic faith, a change that shaped all his later writing. He wrote sacred hymns, historical tragedies and a celebrated ode on Napoleon's death. Honoured as a national figure, he was made a senator in 1860 and died in Milan in 1873.

Manzoni's masterpiece, The Betrothed, first appeared in 1827. Set in Lombardy in the 1620s, it follows two young villagers, Renzo and Lucia, whose marriage is blocked by a powerful nobleman, through famine, revolt and plague. Manzoni revised the language toward educated Florentine speech, and the final 1840 edition helped shape modern standard Italian. Its blend of history, faith, humour and compassion for ordinary people has made it a fixture of Italian schools.
Alexander Hamilton, James Madison & John: Alexander Hamilton, born on the Caribbean island of Nevis, served as George Washington's aide in the Revolutionary War, became the first Secretary of the Treasury, and died in 1804 after a duel with Aaron Burr. James Madison (1751–1836) of Virginia played a central role in drafting the Constitution and became the fourth president. John Jay (1745–1829), a New York lawyer and diplomat, became the first Chief Justice of the United States.

Between 1787 and 1788 the three men published eighty-five essays in New York newspapers under the shared pen name Publius, urging the state to ratify the proposed Constitution. Hamilton wrote the majority, Madison most of the rest, and Jay only a handful after falling ill. The essays explain how a large republic can control factions, why power should be divided among branches, and why an independent judiciary matters. Federalist No. 10 and No. 51 remain among the most studied texts in American political thought.
Alexandre Dumas: Alexandre Dumas was born in 1802 in Villers-Cotterêts, north-east of Paris. His father, Thomas-Alexandre Dumas, the son of a French nobleman and an enslaved woman in Saint-Domingue, became a Revolutionary general but died when Alexandre was a small child. Dumas moved to Paris, found work in the household of the Duke of Orléans and won fame as a playwright with Henri III and His Court in 1829. He earned and spent fortunes, building a lavish château, and died near Dieppe in 1870.

Working with collaborators such as Auguste Maquet, Dumas produced an enormous body of fiction, often serialised in newspapers. The Three Musketeers and The Count of Monte Cristo, both from the 1840s, remain his best-loved books: one a tale of friendship, swordplay and intrigue, the other a vast story of betrayal, imprisonment and revenge. His novels have been adapted countless times for stage and screen, and in 2002 his remains were transferred to the Panthéon in Paris.
Aristotle: Aristotle was born in 384 BC in Stagira, in northern Greece. At about seventeen he went to Athens and joined Plato's Academy, where he remained for some twenty years. After Plato's death he studied animals on the island of Lesbos and was then invited to Macedon to tutor the young Alexander the Great. Returning to Athens, he founded his own school, the Lyceum. He left the city after Alexander's death and died in Chalcis in 322 BC.

His surviving writings, largely lecture notes, cover logic, physics, metaphysics, biology, ethics, politics, rhetoric and poetry. In the Nicomachean Ethics he describes virtue as a balanced middle path and human flourishing as the goal of life; the Politics studies forms of government; the Poetics analyses tragedy. His system of logic dominated Western thought for two thousand years. Medieval scholars in the Islamic world and Christian Europe called him simply the Philosopher, and his ideas remain central to philosophy today.
Arthur Conan Doyle: Arthur Conan Doyle was born in Edinburgh in 1859 into a family of Irish Catholic descent. Educated by Jesuits, he studied medicine at the University of Edinburgh, where his teacher Joseph Bell, famous for his powers of observation, became a model for his greatest creation. He served as a ship's doctor on an Arctic whaler, then set up a medical practice in Southsea. Knighted in 1902, he later became a passionate advocate of spiritualism and died in Crowborough, Sussex, in 1930.

Sherlock Holmes first appeared in A Study in Scarlet in 1887, and the short stories published in The Strand Magazine made Holmes and his friend Dr Watson famous worldwide. Doyle tried to end the series by sending Holmes over the Reichenbach Falls, but public demand brought him back, notably in The Hound of the Baskervilles. Holmes's method of careful observation and deduction shaped detective fiction for generations, and he remains one of the most adapted characters ever created.
Baroness Orczy: Emma Orczy, known as Emmuska, was born in 1865 in Tarnaörs, Hungary, the daughter of Baron Felix Orczy, a landowner and composer. Her family left Hungary when she was a child, living in Brussels and Paris before settling in London. She studied art there and met the illustrator Montagu Barstow, whom she married. Turning to writing to supplement their income, she found enormous success with a historical romance. She died in Henley-on-Thames in 1947.

The Scarlet Pimpernel began as a play written with her husband, first staged in Nottingham in 1903 and in London in 1905, the year the novel appeared. Its hero, Sir Percy Blakeney, seems a foppish aristocrat but secretly rescues French nobles from the guillotine during the Reign of Terror. Orczy also created the armchair detective known as The Old Man in the Corner and Lady Molly of Scotland Yard. Her hero with a secret identity is often seen as an ancestor of later masked heroes such as Zorro.
Benjamin Franklin: Benjamin Franklin was born in Boston in 1706, one of many children of a candle and soap maker. He had little formal schooling and was apprenticed to his older brother, a printer, before running away to Philadelphia at seventeen. There he built a successful printing business, published the Pennsylvania Gazette and helped found a library and the academy that became the University of Pennsylvania. His experiments with electricity made him famous in Europe. He represented the colonies in London, helped draft the Declaration of Independence, secured the French alliance as minister to France, and died in Philadelphia in 1790.

Poor Richard's Almanack, which he published annually from 1732, mixed calendars and weather forecasts with memorable proverbs about thrift, work and good sense. His Autobiography, published after his death, tells the story of a self-made man and became a model for the American ideal of self-improvement. He is still read for his humour, curiosity and portrait of an inventive, public-spirited life.
Bram Stoker: Abraham Stoker was born in 1847 in Clontarf, near Dublin. A sickly child, he was bedridden for years but grew into a strong athlete at Trinity College Dublin. He worked as a civil servant at Dublin Castle and wrote theatre reviews, one of which began a lifelong friendship with the actor Henry Irving. In 1878 he moved to London with his wife, Florence Balcombe, to manage Irving's Lyceum Theatre for decades, writing fiction on the side. He died in London in 1912.

Stoker wrote several novels, including The Lair of the White Worm, but one book overshadows them all. Dracula, published in 1897, tells of a Transylvanian count who travels to England in search of new victims, through diaries, letters and newspaper cuttings. Drawing on vampire folklore and Gothic tradition, it fixed the image of the aristocratic vampire in popular imagination. Through stage plays and films, Count Dracula became one of the most famous figures in horror fiction.
Carlo Collodi: Carlo Lorenzini was born in Florence in 1826 and took his pen name from Collodi, his mother's native village in Tuscany. He studied at a seminary before turning to journalism. A committed patriot, he volunteered in the Italian wars of independence of 1848 and 1859 and founded a satirical newspaper. In the 1870s he translated Perrault's fairy tales into Italian and began writing educational books for children. He died in Florence in 1890.

The Adventures of Pinocchio was serialised in a children's magazine from 1881 and published as a book in 1883. It tells of a wooden puppet carved by the poor Geppetto, who disobeys, tells lies that make his nose grow, and endures many misadventures before becoming a real boy. Funnier, darker and stranger than many later versions, the story mixes social satire with fairy-tale magic. It became one of the most translated Italian books, and Disney's 1940 film made the puppet a global icon.
Charles Darwin: Charles Darwin was born in 1809 in Shrewsbury, England; his grandfathers were the physician Erasmus Darwin and the potter Josiah Wedgwood. He abandoned medicine at Edinburgh and studied at Cambridge, but his real passion was natural history. From 1831 to 1836 he sailed around the world as naturalist on HMS Beagle, collecting specimens and observing wildlife, notably in the Galápagos Islands. He then married his cousin Emma Wedgwood and settled at Down House in Kent, where he worked despite chronic illness. He died in 1882 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.

He spent two decades developing his theory of evolution and was prompted to publish when Alfred Russel Wallace reached similar conclusions. On the Origin of Species, published in 1859, argued that species change over time through natural selection. The Descent of Man followed in 1871. Written in clear prose for general readers, his books transformed biology and changed how humanity understands its place in nature.
Charles Dickens: Charles Dickens was born in 1812 in Portsmouth, England. When he was twelve his father was imprisoned for debt, and Charles was sent to work in a blacking factory, an experience of poverty and shame that marked him for life. He later worked as a law clerk and a parliamentary reporter before publishing humorous sketches under the name Boz. The Pickwick Papers, issued in monthly parts in 1836 and 1837, made him famous. He edited magazines, gave hugely popular public readings, and died at Gad's Hill, Kent, in 1870; he was buried in Westminster Abbey.

Oliver Twist exposed the cruelty of workhouses, A Christmas Carol created Ebenezer Scrooge, and David Copperfield drew on his own youth. Later works such as Bleak House, Little Dorrit, A Tale of Two Cities and Great Expectations combine intricate plots with sharp social criticism. Dickens filled his books with unforgettable characters, comedy and pathos, and he helped bring attention to child labour, poverty and injustice.
Charles Mackay: Charles Mackay was born in Perth, Scotland, in 1814 and spent part of his youth in Belgium, where he became fluent in French. He built his career in journalism, working for the London Morning Chronicle, editing the Glasgow Argus and later the Illustrated London News. He was also a popular poet and songwriter. He died in London in 1889.

Mackay's lasting fame rests on Memoirs of Extraordinary Popular Delusions, first published in 1841 and now usually known as Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds. In lively chapters he described financial manias such as the Mississippi Scheme, the South Sea Bubble and Dutch tulip mania, alongside alchemy, fortune-telling, witch hunts and the Crusades. Modern historians have questioned some of his accounts, especially of the tulip craze, but his central theme, that people can lose their judgment together, still resonates. The book is widely read by investors and anyone curious about crowd behaviour.
Charlotte Brontë: Charlotte Brontë was born in 1816 in Thornton, Yorkshire, the daughter of Patrick Brontë, an Irish-born clergyman, and the family soon moved to the parsonage at Haworth. Her mother died when she was five, and her two elder sisters died after attending a harsh boarding school. She worked as a teacher and governess and studied in Brussels. After the deaths of all her siblings by 1849, she married Arthur Bell Nicholls in 1854 and died in 1855, during pregnancy.

In 1846 the sisters published a volume of poems under the names Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell. Charlotte's novel Jane Eyre followed in 1847 and was an immediate success. Its story of an orphaned governess who insists on her own dignity, told in a passionate first-person voice, broke new ground. She went on to write Shirley and Villette, which draws on her time in Brussels, while The Professor appeared after her death. It remains one of the most loved English novels.
Daniel Defoe: Daniel Foe, who later called himself Defoe, was born in London around 1660, the son of a tallow chandler. His family were Dissenters, Protestants outside the Church of England, so he attended a Dissenting academy rather than a university. He became a merchant, went bankrupt, and took part in the Duke of Monmouth's rebellion of 1685. He was pilloried and imprisoned for a satire on religious intolerance, then worked as a political writer and secret agent for ministers. He died in London in 1731.

Defoe wrote hundreds of works, including the journal The Review, but he turned to fiction late in life. Robinson Crusoe, published in 1719 when he was nearly sixty, tells of a sailor shipwrecked alone on an island for many years. Moll Flanders and A Journal of the Plague Year followed in 1722, and Roxana in 1724. Written as convincing first-person accounts full of practical detail, these books helped establish the realistic novel in English.
Dante Alighieri: Dante Alighieri was born in Florence in 1265. As a boy he met Beatrice Portinari, whose memory inspired much of his poetry even after her early death. He took an active part in Florentine politics and served as one of the city's priors. In 1302, when a rival faction seized power, he was exiled and condemned to death should he return. He spent the rest of his life moving among Italian courts and died in Ravenna in 1321, where he is buried.

Dante's early work La Vita Nuova tells of his love for Beatrice in prose and verse. In exile he wrote treatises and above all the Divine Comedy, an epic in three parts: Inferno, Purgatorio and Paradiso. Guided by the Roman poet Virgil and then by Beatrice, Dante journeys through the afterlife, meeting historical and contemporary figures. Written in Tuscan rather than Latin, in interlocking three-line stanzas, the poem helped make the Florentine dialect the basis of modern Italian.
David Ricardo: David Ricardo was born in London in 1772 into a Sephardic Jewish family that had come from the Netherlands. His father was a stockbroker, whom David joined at fourteen. At twenty-one he married a Quaker, which led to a break with his family, and he grew extremely wealthy through stockbroking and government loans. After reading Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations he grew fascinated by economics and became friends with Thomas Malthus and James Mill. He entered Parliament in 1819 and died in 1823, aged only fifty-one.

Ricardo's major book, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, appeared in 1817. It set out theories of rent, distribution and value. Most famously, it explained comparative advantage: using the example of England and Portugal trading cloth and wine, Ricardo showed that two countries can both gain from trade even if one is better at producing everything. His rigorous, abstract method shaped classical economics, and comparative advantage remains a cornerstone of trade theory.
E. Nesbit: Edith Nesbit was born in 1858 in Kennington, London. Her father, an agricultural chemist, died when she was three. In 1880 she married Hubert Bland, and the couple were among the founders of the socialist Fabian Society. Their household was unconventional and often short of money, and Nesbit wrote poems, stories and journalism to support the family. Success came in her forties with books for children, published under the name E. Nesbit. She died in Kent in 1924.

The Story of the Treasure Seekers appeared in 1899, followed by Five Children and It, The Phoenix and the Carpet, The Railway Children and The Enchanted Castle. Nesbit wrote about lively, quarrelsome, believable children and placed magic in the middle of ordinary family life, often with comic results. Later fantasy writers, including C. S. Lewis, acknowledged her influence, and The Railway Children in particular has remained a much-loved classic on page and screen.
Edith Wharton: Edith Newbold Jones was born in New York City in 1862 into a wealthy, long-established family. In 1885 she married Edward Wharton; the marriage was unhappy and ended in divorce in 1913. She designed and built a country house, The Mount, in Massachusetts, and was a close friend of Henry James. From 1907 she lived mainly in France, where she organised refugee relief during the First World War and received the Legion of Honour. She died in France in 1937.

The House of Mirth, published in 1905, follows Lily Bart's struggle to survive in a society that values women for marriage and money. Ethan Frome is a stark tale of rural New England, and The Custom of the Country satirises social ambition. The Age of Innocence, a portrait of old New York in the 1870s, won the Pulitzer Prize in 1921, making her the first woman to receive it for fiction. Her sharp irony keeps her widely read.
Edmondo De Amicis: Edmondo De Amicis was born in 1846 in Oneglia, on the Ligurian coast of Italy. He trained at the military academy in Modena and served as an army officer, fighting at the battle of Custoza in 1866 during the wars that unified Italy. He then turned to journalism, publishing popular sketches of military life, and travelled widely, writing much-read books about Spain, Morocco, Holland and Constantinople. In later life he embraced socialism. He died in Bordighera in 1908.

Cuore, published in 1886, takes the form of a school-year diary kept by Enrico, a boy in Turin, with monthly stories told in class. The book aimed to teach the children of a newly united Italy about duty, sacrifice, kindness and love of country, bringing together pupils from different regions and social classes. It was an immediate success, was translated into many languages, and shaped generations of Italian readers. It is still remembered for its warmth and emotion.
Emily Brontë: Emily Brontë was born in 1818 in Thornton, Yorkshire, and grew up in the parsonage at Haworth. With her younger sister Anne she created the imaginary kingdom of Gondal, writing poems and stories set there for years. Intensely private and homesick whenever away, she worked briefly as a teacher and studied in Brussels with Charlotte in 1842. In 1846 her poems appeared under the name Ellis Bell. She died of tuberculosis in December 1848, aged thirty, soon after the death of her brother Branwell.

Emily's only novel, Wuthering Heights, was published in 1847. Told largely by the housekeeper Nelly Dean, it traces the fierce bond between Catherine Earnshaw and the foundling Heathcliff and the revenge that follows. Many early reviewers found it shocking, but its daring structure and raw emotional force eventually won it recognition as one of the greatest English novels. Her poetry, including No Coward Soul Is Mine, is also highly regarded.
F. Scott Fitzgerald: Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald was born in 1896 in St Paul, Minnesota. He studied at Princeton but left without a degree and joined the army in 1917. While stationed in Alabama he met Zelda Sayre, and after his first novel, This Side of Paradise, succeeded in 1920, they married and became celebrities. Later years brought financial trouble, heavy drinking and Zelda's mental illness. Fitzgerald moved to Hollywood to write screenplays, and he died there of a heart attack in 1940, aged forty-four.

Fitzgerald's story collection Tales of the Jazz Age helped give the 1920s their name. The Great Gatsby, published in 1925, tells of the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby and his longing for Daisy Buchanan, as seen by the narrator Nick Carraway. Its lyrical prose and portrait of wealth, desire and disillusion made it a defining American novel. He also wrote Tender Is the Night, the unfinished The Last Tycoon and many short stories, including Babylon Revisited.
Frances Hodgson Burnett: Frances Hodgson was born in Manchester, England, in 1849. Her father died when she was small, and in 1865 the struggling family emigrated to Tennessee. There she began selling stories to magazines to help support the household. She married Swan Burnett, a doctor, and had two sons; the death of her elder son Lionel in 1890 was a great sorrow. She divided her life between Britain and the United States, for some years tending a beloved garden at Great Maytham Hall in Kent. She died on Long Island, New York, in 1924.

Little Lord Fauntleroy, published in 1886, was a huge success. A Little Princess tells of Sara Crewe, who keeps her kindness and imagination after losing her fortune. The Secret Garden, from 1911, follows lonely Mary Lennox as she restores a hidden garden and finds friendship and healing. Its themes of nature, growth and renewal have made it one of the most beloved children's novels.
Franz Kafka: Franz Kafka was born in Prague in 1883, then part of Austria-Hungary, into a German-speaking Jewish family. His relationship with his domineering father, a successful merchant, troubled him all his life. He earned a law doctorate and worked for most of his career at an accident insurance institute, writing at night. In 1917 he was diagnosed with tuberculosis, and he died in a sanatorium near Vienna in 1924. He asked his friend Max Brod to burn his unpublished manuscripts, but Brod published them instead.

In his lifetime Kafka published only a few stories, including The Metamorphosis, in which a salesman wakes up transformed into a giant insect. His novels The Trial, The Castle and Amerika appeared after his death. In clear, precise prose, he describes bewildered individuals facing incomprehensible authority, guilt and isolation. He is now regarded as one of the most important writers of the twentieth century, and the word Kafkaesque entered many languages.
Fyodor Dostoevsky: Fyodor Dostoevsky was born in Moscow in 1821, the son of a doctor at a hospital for the poor. He trained as a military engineer in St Petersburg but left the service to write, and his first novel, Poor Folk, was warmly received in 1846. In 1849 he was arrested for joining a radical discussion circle, subjected to a mock execution, and sentenced to four years of hard labour in Siberia. He struggled with epilepsy, gambling and debt. He died in St Petersburg in 1881.

Dostoevsky drew on his prison years in The House of the Dead, and Notes from Underground introduced a bitter, self-contradicting narrator. His great novels followed: Crime and Punishment, about a poor student who commits murder to test a theory; The Idiot; Demons; and The Brothers Karamazov, which wrestles with faith, doubt and responsibility. His psychological depth influenced existentialist philosophers and countless novelists, and his books remain among the most powerful explorations of the human conscience.
Gaston Leroux: Gaston Leroux was born in Paris in 1868 and grew up in Normandy. He studied law and worked as a court reporter before becoming an international correspondent for the newspaper Le Matin, covering events such as the 1905 revolution in Russia. Around 1907 he left journalism to devote himself to fiction, writing novels, serials and plays at a rapid pace. He died in Nice in 1927.

Leroux first made his name with The Mystery of the Yellow Room, a celebrated locked-room puzzle featuring the young reporter-detective Joseph Rouletabille. The Phantom of the Opera, serialised in 1909 and 1910, is set in the Paris Opera House and tells of a masked, disfigured genius who haunts its cellars and falls in love with the singer Christine Daaé. The novel blends mystery, romance and Gothic horror. It was only moderately successful at first, but the 1925 silent film and later Andrew Lloyd Webber's long-running musical made the Phantom known around the world.
Geoffrey Chaucer: Geoffrey Chaucer was born in London around 1343, the son of a wine merchant. As a youth he served in an aristocratic household and fought in France, where he was captured and ransomed. He went on to a long career in royal service, including as controller of customs for the port of London, and travelled on missions to Italy, where he encountered the works of Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio. He died in 1400 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.

His early poems include The Book of the Duchess, and his Troilus and Criseyde is a moving tale of love set in the Trojan War. His most famous work, the unfinished Canterbury Tales, imagines pilgrims travelling to Canterbury who tell stories to pass the time. Pilgrims such as the knight, the miller and the Wife of Bath reveal themselves through tales ranging from courtly romance to bawdy comedy. Writing in English when French and Latin dominated, Chaucer showed what the language could do.
George Eliot: Mary Ann Evans was born in 1819 on an estate in Warwickshire, where her father worked as land agent. A brilliant student, she lost her evangelical faith as a young woman, causing a painful rift with her father. She translated German theological works and moved to London, where she became assistant editor of the Westminster Review. She lived openly for over twenty years with the married writer George Henry Lewes, which scandalised society. She married John Cross in 1880 and died in London months later.

Eliot's first fiction, Scenes of Clerical Life, was followed by Adam Bede, The Mill on the Floss and Silas Marner. Middlemarch, published in 1871 and 1872, portrays the lives of a provincial town with extraordinary breadth and sympathy, following Dorothea Brooke, the doctor Lydgate and many others. Her final novel, Daniel Deronda, explores Jewish identity. Eliot combined realism with deep moral insight, and Middlemarch is often named among the greatest novels in English.
Giovanni Boccaccio: Giovanni Boccaccio was born in 1313, probably in Florence or nearby Certaldo, the illegitimate son of a merchant. As a young man he was sent to Naples to learn banking and canon law, but preferred literature and court life. He returned to Florence around 1341 and lived through the Black Death of 1348, which killed a large part of the city's population. He became a close friend of Petrarch, carried out diplomatic missions for Florence, and in his final years gave public lectures on Dante. He died in Certaldo in 1375.

Boccaccio's masterpiece, the Decameron, frames one hundred stories told by ten young Florentines who escape the plague to a country villa. The tales range from witty and bawdy to tragic and noble, offering a vivid picture of merchants, lovers, clergy and tricksters. His earlier poems supplied plots for Chaucer, and his Latin works, including lives of famous women and a guide to classical mythology, helped spread Renaissance humanism.
Giovanni Verga: Giovanni Verga was born in 1840 in Catania, Sicily, into a landowning family. He abandoned law studies to write, moving to Florence in 1865 and later to Milan. His early novels were sentimental, romantic stories, such as Story of a Blackcap. In later life he returned to Catania, where he lived quietly. He was made a senator in 1920 and died in his home town in 1922.

In the 1870s Verga turned to a new style, inspired partly by French naturalism, that became known as verismo. His stories in Life in the Fields, including Cavalleria rusticana, which Mascagni turned into a famous opera, and the novels I Malavoglia and Mastro-don Gesualdo portray Sicilian fishermen, peasants and landowners struggling against poverty and fate. Verga tried to let his characters speak for themselves, reducing the narrator's presence and using the rhythms of their speech. His impersonal technique and compassion for the defeated made him a key figure in modern Italian fiction.
Gustave Flaubert: Gustave Flaubert was born in Rouen in 1821, the son of the chief surgeon at the city hospital. After a seizure in 1844 he abandoned law studies in Paris and settled with his family at Croisset, near Rouen, where he wrote for the rest of his life. When Madame Bovary was serialised, he was put on trial for offending public morals and was acquitted. He was a mentor to the young Guy de Maupassant and died at Croisset in 1880.

Madame Bovary, published as a book in 1857, tells of Emma Bovary, a doctor's wife in provincial Normandy whose romantic dreams lead to adultery, debt and ruin. Flaubert worked painstakingly on every sentence in search of the exact word, and his cool, precise narration became a model for realist fiction. He also wrote Salammbô, Sentimental Education and Three Tales. His devotion to style influenced novelists from Henry James onward, and Madame Bovary is often counted among the greatest novels.
Guy de Maupassant: Guy de Maupassant was born in Normandy in 1850 and grew up mainly with his mother after his parents separated. He served in the Franco-Prussian War and then worked as a clerk in government ministries in Paris. Gustave Flaubert, a friend of his mother, took him under his wing and guided his writing. In the 1880s he was enormously productive, but syphilis gradually destroyed his health. After a suicide attempt in 1892 he was confined to a clinic in Paris, where he died in 1893.

Maupassant became famous in 1880 with Boule de Suif, a story of a prostitute travelling with respectable citizens during the Prussian occupation. In little more than a decade he wrote around three hundred stories, including The Necklace and Le Horla, and novels such as Bel-Ami. His tales are economical, ironic and clear-eyed, often ending with a sharp twist. He shaped the modern short story and influenced writers around the world.
H. G. Wells: Herbert George Wells was born in 1866 in Bromley, Kent, into a struggling family of shopkeepers. He was apprenticed to a draper, an experience he hated, before winning a scholarship to study science in London, where he was taught by Thomas Henry Huxley. He worked as a teacher and journalist before his fiction made him famous. A socialist, he joined the Fabian Society and wrote widely about politics, history and the future of humanity. He died in London in 1946.

Wells's early scientific romances helped create modern science fiction. The Time Machine, The Island of Doctor Moreau, The Invisible Man and The War of the Worlds explored time travel, scientific cruelty and alien invasion. He also wrote comic novels about ordinary lives, such as Kipps and The History of Mr Polly, and the popular Outline of History. His ideas about time travel, alien invasion and technology still shape stories, films and the way we imagine the future.
Hans Christian Andersen: Hans Christian Andersen was born in 1805 in Odense, Denmark, the son of a poor shoemaker and a washerwoman. After his father's death he left for Copenhagen at fourteen, hoping to become an actor or singer. He failed on the stage, but influential patrons, especially Jonas Collin, arranged for him to attend grammar school. He travelled widely across Europe, writing novels, plays, travel books and an autobiography. He never married, and he died in Copenhagen in 1875.

Andersen published his first small booklet of fairy tales in 1835 and wrote well over a hundred more. Unlike the Grimms, he invented most of his stories, among them The Emperor's New Clothes, The Little Mermaid, The Ugly Duckling, The Snow Queen and The Little Match Girl. He wrote in a conversational style that appealed to children and adults alike, blending humour, sadness and moral insight. His tales have been translated into a great many languages and inspired ballets, films and picture books.
Harriet Beecher Stowe: Harriet Beecher was born in 1811 in Litchfield, Connecticut, one of the many children of the Calvinist preacher Lyman Beecher. She taught at her sister Catharine's school in Hartford, then moved to Cincinnati, across the river from slave-holding Kentucky, where she met people who had escaped slavery. She married Calvin Stowe, a professor of theology, and raised seven children. The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 moved her to write. She later lived in Hartford and died there in 1896.

Uncle Tom's Cabin was serialised in an anti-slavery newspaper and published as a book in 1852. It follows the gentle, enslaved Tom and the escaping Eliza, exposing the cruelty of slavery. It became the best-selling novel of the nineteenth century and deeply influenced public opinion before the Civil War. Later readers have criticised its racial stereotypes, and the phrase Uncle Tom took on a negative meaning. She also wrote Dred and novels of New England life.
Henry David Thoreau: Henry David Thoreau was born in 1817 in Concord, Massachusetts, where his family made pencils. He graduated from Harvard in 1837, taught school with his brother, and became a friend and protégé of Ralph Waldo Emerson, joining the Transcendentalist circle. From July 1845 to September 1847 he lived in a small cabin he built at Walden Pond, on land owned by Emerson. In 1846 he spent a night in jail for refusing to pay a poll tax in protest against slavery. He worked as a surveyor, opposed slavery, and died in Concord of tuberculosis in 1862.

Thoreau's essay Resistance to Civil Government, later known as Civil Disobedience, argued that individuals should refuse to cooperate with unjust laws. Walden, published in 1854, reflects on his life in the woods, on simplicity, self-reliance and close observation of nature. His ideas on peaceful resistance influenced Mahatma Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr., and his writing on nature inspired the environmental movement.
Herman Melville: Herman Melville was born in New York City in 1819. His father's business failed, and he died when Herman was twelve. After working as a clerk and teacher, Melville went to sea, eventually on a whaler in the Pacific. He deserted in the Marquesas Islands and returned home on a navy frigate. He married Elizabeth Shaw and befriended Nathaniel Hawthorne. Later he worked for nineteen years as a customs inspector in New York, where he died in 1891, largely forgotten.

Melville's first books, Typee and Omoo, drew on his South Sea adventures and were popular. Moby-Dick, published in 1851, tells of Captain Ahab's obsessive hunt for a white whale, mixing adventure, philosophy and whaling lore; it sold poorly. He went on to write stories such as Bartleby, the Scrivener, the novel The Confidence-Man, and Billy Budd, published only in 1924. A revival in the 1920s established Moby-Dick as one of the great American novels.
Homer: Nothing about Homer's life can be known for certain. The ancient Greeks believed he was a blind poet from Ionia, on the coast of Asia Minor, and several cities, including Smyrna and Chios, claimed him as their own. Modern scholars debate whether a single poet composed both great epics or whether they grew out of a long tradition of oral storytelling. The poems probably took shape in the eighth or seventh century BC and were written down later.

The Iliad tells of the anger of Achilles during the final year of the Trojan War and its tragic consequences for Greeks and Trojans alike. The Odyssey follows the clever Odysseus on his long journey home to Ithaca and his wife Penelope after the war. Composed in hexameter verse, rich in vivid similes and repeated epithets, the poems were central to Greek education. They inspired Virgil's Aeneid, countless later poets and artists, and modern works such as James Joyce's Ulysses.
Honoré de Balzac: Honoré de Balzac was born in Tours in 1799. He studied law in Paris and worked as a clerk, but was determined to write. His early pseudonymous novels failed, and business ventures in printing left him with debts that pursued him all his life. He wrote at a ferocious pace, often through the night, fuelled by coffee. For many years he corresponded with the Polish countess Ewelina Hańska, whom he finally married in 1850, only months before his death in Paris that August.

Balzac gathered his novels and stories under the title La Comédie humaine, a vast portrait of French society after the Revolution. Works such as Eugénie Grandet, Father Goriot, Lost Illusions and Cousin Bette show bankers, misers, ambitious young men, aristocrats and criminals driven by money and passion. He was among the first to use recurring characters, such as the ambitious Rastignac and the criminal Vautrin, across many books. His realism influenced later novelists, including Zola and Proust.
J. M. Barrie: James Matthew Barrie was born in 1860 in Kirriemuir, Scotland, the son of a weaver. When he was six, his older brother David died in a skating accident, and his mother's grief marked him deeply. He studied at Edinburgh University and worked as a journalist before moving to London. He found success with tales of Scottish village life and stage comedies. His friendship with the Llewelyn Davies family inspired Peter Pan, and he later became guardian of their five sons. He died in London in 1937.

Peter Pan first appeared in The Little White Bird in 1902; the play opened in London in 1904 and later became the novel Peter and Wendy. The story of the boy who takes Wendy and her brothers to Neverland, with fairies, pirates and Captain Hook, became a lasting classic. His other plays include The Admirable Crichton and Mary Rose. In 1929 he gave the rights to Peter Pan to Great Ormond Street children's hospital.
Jack London: Jack London was born in San Francisco in 1876 and grew up in poverty around Oakland. As a teenager he worked in factories, raided oyster beds, sailed to the Pacific on a sealing schooner and tramped across the country, becoming a committed socialist. After a short time at the University of California, he joined the Klondike Gold Rush in 1897. He became one of the best-paid writers of his day and died at his California ranch in 1916, aged forty.

London's fame began with stories of the Yukon. The Call of the Wild, published in 1903, follows Buck, a stolen dog who answers the call of his wild ancestry; White Fang reverses the journey. He also wrote The Sea-Wolf, the dystopian The Iron Heel, the semi-autobiographical Martin Eden, and stories such as To Build a Fire. His vigorous prose about survival, nature and social struggle made him one of the most widely read and translated American authors.
Jacob & Wilhelm Grimm: Jacob Grimm was born in 1785 and Wilhelm in 1786, both in Hanau, Germany. Their father died when they were children, leaving the family poor. They studied law at Marburg, where Friedrich Carl von Savigny inspired their interest in old German texts. After working as librarians in Kassel, they became professors at Göttingen but were dismissed in 1837 for protesting the king's abolition of the constitution, and moved to Berlin. Wilhelm married, but the brothers lived and worked together; Wilhelm died in 1859 and Jacob in 1863.

The first volume of their Children's and Household Tales appeared in 1812, and the collection grew through seven editions to some two hundred tales. It includes Cinderella, Rumpelstiltskin, Snow White and Hansel and Gretel. Gathered from friends and informants to preserve German folk tradition, the tales became known worldwide. Jacob also helped found historical linguistics, describing the sound changes known as Grimm's law, and the brothers began a huge German dictionary.
James Fenimore Cooper: James Fenimore Cooper was born in 1789 in Burlington, New Jersey, and grew up in Cooperstown, New York, the frontier settlement founded by his father. He was expelled from Yale, served as a merchant sailor and then as a midshipman in the United States Navy. After marrying Susan DeLancey he began writing in his thirties, and his novel The Spy brought him success in 1821. After several years in Europe he returned to Cooperstown, where he died in 1851.

Cooper's best-known works are the five Leatherstocking Tales, centred on the frontiersman Natty Bumppo, also called Hawkeye. They include The Pioneers, The Prairie, The Pathfinder, The Deerslayer and, above all, The Last of the Mohicans, set during the French and Indian War. He also helped invent the American sea novel with The Pilot. Although critics, including Mark Twain, mocked his style, Cooper was one of the first American novelists to win international fame and shaped lasting images of the frontier.
James Joyce: James Joyce was born in 1882 in Rathgar, Dublin, the eldest surviving child of a large family whose fortunes steadily declined. He was educated by Jesuits and at University College Dublin. In 1904 he left Ireland with Nora Barnacle, his lifelong partner and later wife, living in Trieste, Zurich and, from 1920, Paris. He suffered serious eye trouble. Though he never returned to live in Ireland, Dublin is the setting of all his fiction. He died in Zurich in 1941.

Dubliners, published in 1914, is a collection of stories about ordinary Dublin lives, ending with the celebrated The Dead. A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man follows the growth of Stephen Dedalus as a young writer. Ulysses, published in 1922, recounts a single day, 16 June 1904, mirroring Homer's Odyssey and pushing stream of consciousness to new limits. Finnegans Wake followed in 1939. Joyce transformed the novel and remains central to modernist literature.
Jane Austen: Jane Austen was born in 1775 at Steventon rectory in Hampshire, the seventh of eight children of the Reverend George Austen. Educated mostly at home in a lively, bookish family, she began writing comic pieces as a girl. The family moved to Bath in 1801 and, after her father's death, settled in 1809 in a cottage at Chawton provided by her brother Edward. She died in Winchester in 1817, aged forty-one, and was buried in the cathedral.

Austen published Sense and Sensibility in 1811, Pride and Prejudice in 1813, Mansfield Park in 1814 and Emma in 1815; Northanger Abbey and Persuasion appeared after her death. Focusing on a few families in country villages, her novels follow young women navigating love, money, marriage and social expectation. She wrote with sharp irony, sparkling dialogue and a pioneering technique of letting the narrator slip into a character's thoughts. Her books remain hugely popular and are adapted again and again.
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe: Johann Wolfgang Goethe was born in 1749 in Frankfurt am Main into a prosperous family. He studied law at Leipzig and Strasbourg and became famous almost overnight with The Sorrows of Young Werther in 1774. The following year Duke Karl August invited him to Weimar, where he served for decades as a minister. A long journey to Italy from 1786 to 1788 renewed his art. He was also a dedicated scientist, studying plants, anatomy and colour. He died in Weimar in 1832.

Werther, the tale of a sensitive young man destroyed by unrequited love, was a sensation across Europe. His other works include the novels Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship and Elective Affinities. His masterpiece is Faust, published in two parts in 1808 and 1832, the drama of a scholar who makes a pact with the devil Mephistopheles in his restless hunger for knowledge and experience. Goethe championed the idea of world literature, and he remains the towering figure of German letters.
John Bunyan: John Bunyan was born in 1628 in Elstow, near Bedford, the son of a tinker, and followed his father's trade. As a teenager he served in the Parliamentary army during the English Civil War. He later went through a long spiritual crisis, joined an independent church in Bedford and became a popular preacher. After the Restoration in 1660 he was arrested for preaching without a licence and spent about twelve years in Bedford gaol. Released in 1672, he became a leading Nonconformist pastor. He died in London in 1688.

Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners recounts his own spiritual struggles. The Pilgrim's Progress, published in 1678, is an allegory in which Christian journeys from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City, passing through the Slough of Despond and Vanity Fair. Written in plain, vivid English, it became one of the most widely read books in the language and has been translated into many languages.
John Locke: John Locke was born in 1632 in Wrington, Somerset, England, the son of a lawyer who fought for Parliament in the Civil War. He studied at Westminster School and Christ Church, Oxford, including medicine. He became physician, adviser and friend to Anthony Ashley Cooper, later Earl of Shaftesbury, a leading opposition politician. Under suspicion, he fled to the Netherlands in 1683, returning after the Glorious Revolution. He later held government posts and died in Essex in 1704.

In An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Locke argued that the mind begins as a blank slate and that all knowledge comes from experience, laying foundations for empiricism. His Two Treatises of Government argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property and that government rests on the consent of the governed. He also wrote A Letter Concerning Toleration and Some Thoughts Concerning Education. His ideas deeply influenced the Enlightenment and the American founders.
John Milton: John Milton was born in London in 1608, the son of a scrivener who was also a composer. He studied at St Paul's School and Christ's College, Cambridge, and travelled in Italy, where he met Galileo. During the conflicts of the 1640s he wrote pamphlets against bishops, in favour of divorce and in defence of a free press. Under the Commonwealth he served as Latin secretary to the Council of State, and by the early 1650s he was blind. He died in London in 1674.

Milton's early poems include L'Allegro, Il Penseroso, the masque Comus and the elegy Lycidas. His prose tract Areopagitica remains a classic defence of freedom of the press. Paradise Lost, first published in 1667 and dictated after he lost his sight, is an epic in blank verse telling the story of Satan's rebellion and the fall of Adam and Eve. He also wrote Paradise Regained and Samson Agonistes, and he ranks among the greatest English poets.
John Stuart Mill: John Stuart Mill was born in London in 1806, the son of the philosopher James Mill, who gave him an intensive education beginning with Greek at three. At twenty he suffered a mental crisis and found relief in poetry, especially Wordsworth's. His long friendship with Harriet Taylor, whom he married in 1851, shaped his thinking. As a Member of Parliament he proposed giving women the vote. He died in Avignon, France, in 1873.

Mill's A System of Logic and Principles of Political Economy were major textbooks of their time. On Liberty, published in 1859, argues that society may limit individual freedom only to prevent harm to others and defends free thought and discussion. Utilitarianism refines Bentham's idea that actions should promote happiness, distinguishing higher from lower pleasures. The Subjection of Women makes a powerful case for equality between the sexes, and his Autobiography describes his unusual upbringing. His clear arguments for liberty and equality remain central to modern political debate.
Jonathan Swift: Jonathan Swift was born in Dublin in 1667 to English parents; his father died before he was born. He studied at Trinity College Dublin and then worked as secretary to the statesman Sir William Temple in England. He was ordained in the Church of Ireland and became a leading political writer for the Tory government in London. In 1713 he was appointed Dean of St Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin, a post he held until his death. He died in Dublin in 1745.

Swift's early satire A Tale of a Tub mocked religious extremes. His most famous book, Gulliver's Travels, published in 1726, sends its hero to Lilliput, Brobdingnag, Laputa and the land of the rational horses called Houyhnhnms, satirising politics, science and human pride. A Modest Proposal, from 1729, ironically suggests that the poor of Ireland sell their children as food, a savage attack on the treatment of the Irish poor. Swift is considered the foremost prose satirist in English.
Joseph Conrad: Józef Teodor Konrad Korzeniowski was born in 1857 in Berdychiv, then in the Russian Empire, to Polish parents. His father, a writer and patriot, was exiled for political activity, and Conrad was orphaned by eleven. At sixteen he went to sea from Marseilles, later rising to captain in the British merchant navy. A voyage up the Congo River in 1890 left a deep impression. English was his third language, yet he became one of its great stylists. He settled in Kent and died there in 1924.

Conrad's first novel, Almayer's Folly, appeared in 1895. Heart of Darkness, narrated by the sailor Marlow, follows a journey into colonial Africa in search of the ivory trader Kurtz; Chinua Achebe famously criticised its portrayal of Africans. Lord Jim explores guilt and honour, and The Secret Agent deals with terrorism in London. Using shifting narrators and complex timelines, Conrad examined isolation, moral failure and imperialism, and he influenced many later novelists.
Jules Verne: Jules Verne was born in 1828 in the port city of Nantes, France, the son of a lawyer. He studied law in Paris but was drawn to the theatre, writing plays and reading widely in science and geography. In 1863 the publisher Pierre-Jules Hetzel published Five Weeks in a Balloon and signed him for a long series of novels. Verne settled in Amiens, served on the town council and died there in 1905.

Verne's series of Extraordinary Voyages combined adventure with scientific and geographical detail. Journey to the Centre of the Earth, From the Earth to the Moon, Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea, with the enigmatic Captain Nemo and his submarine Nautilus, and Around the World in Eighty Days, with the punctual Phileas Fogg, are among the best known. His imaginative use of technology made him a pioneer of science fiction, and he is one of the most translated authors in the world.
Kahlil Gibran: Gibran Khalil Gibran was born in 1883 in Bsharri, in the mountains of what is now Lebanon, then part of the Ottoman Empire. His family was poor, and in 1895 his mother emigrated with her children to Boston. He returned to Beirut for schooling in Arabic, then came back to Boston, where he soon lost his sister, half-brother and mother. With the support of his patron Mary Haskell he studied art in Paris. He settled in New York, where he died in 1931.

Gibran first wrote in Arabic, publishing stories, poems and the novel The Broken Wings, and became an important figure in modern Arabic literature. He later wrote in English, starting with The Madman. The Prophet, published in 1923, presents the farewell teachings of the wise man Almustafa on love, marriage, children, work, freedom, joy, sorrow and death, in poetic prose that Gibran illustrated himself. Its spiritual warmth and universal themes have kept it popular for generations.
Karl Marx: Karl Marx was born in 1818 in Trier, in the Prussian Rhineland, the son of a lawyer of Jewish descent. He studied law and philosophy at Bonn and Berlin and received his doctorate in 1841. He edited a radical newspaper that the authorities soon closed. Moving to Paris, he met Friedrich Engels, his lifelong collaborator. Expelled from several countries, he settled in London in 1849 with his wife, Jenny von Westphalen, often living in poverty. He died in London in 1883.

With Engels, Marx wrote The Communist Manifesto in 1848. His other works include The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte and above all Capital, whose first volume appeared in 1867. Marx analysed capitalism as a historical system driven by the exploitation of labour, argued that history is shaped by class struggle and economic forces, and predicted the system's collapse. His ideas inspired movements and revolutions that reshaped the twentieth century and remain essential reading in the social sciences.
Karl Marx & Friedrich Engels: Karl Marx was born in Trier in 1818 and studied law and philosophy before turning to radical journalism. Friedrich Engels, born in 1820 in Barmen, the son of a textile manufacturer, worked at his family's cotton business in Manchester and wrote The Condition of the Working Class in England. The two men met in Paris in 1844 and began a partnership that lasted for life. After 1848 both settled in England, where Engels supported Marx financially for years. Marx died in London in 1883, Engels in 1895.

Published in London in February 1848 for the Communist League, The Communist Manifesto declared that history is the history of class struggles and called on workers to unite. After Marx's death, Engels edited the remaining volumes of Capital and wrote popular works such as Socialism: Utopian and Scientific. Their ideas became the foundation of Marxism, and the Manifesto remains one of the most influential political texts ever written.
Kenneth Grahame: Kenneth Grahame was born in Edinburgh in 1859. His mother died when he was small, and he was raised by his grandmother at Cookham Dean, near the River Thames. Unable to afford university, he joined the Bank of England and rose to become its Secretary before retiring in 1908. He married Elspeth Thomson, and their only son, Alastair, died young while a student at Oxford. Grahame died at Pangbourne, on the Thames, in 1932.

Grahame first became known for nostalgic books about childhood, The Golden Age and Dream Days. The Wind in the Willows, published in 1908, grew out of bedtime stories and letters for his son. It follows the gentle Mole, the river-loving Rat, the wise Badger and the boastful, car-crazy Toad of Toad Hall. Mixing comedy, adventure and a lyrical love of the English countryside, it became a children's classic. A. A. Milne adapted it for the stage as Toad of Toad Hall.
L. Frank Baum: Lyman Frank Baum was born in 1856 in Chittenango, New York, the son of a prosperous businessman. As a young man he bred poultry, acted and wrote plays. In 1882 he married Maud Gage, daughter of the suffragist Matilda Joslyn Gage. He ran a store and a newspaper in Dakota Territory, then moved to Chicago, where he worked as a reporter and salesman. He later moved to Hollywood, where he died in 1919.

Baum's first children's books were Mother Goose in Prose and Father Goose. The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, published in 1900 with illustrations by W. W. Denslow, tells of Dorothy, swept from Kansas to the magical land of Oz, where she meets the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman and the Cowardly Lion. It was so popular that Baum wrote thirteen more Oz books. The 1939 film made Oz world famous. Baum is often credited with creating one of the first great American fairy tales.
L. M. Montgomery: Lucy Maud Montgomery was born in 1874 in Clifton, Prince Edward Island, Canada. Her mother died before she was two, and she was raised by her grandparents in Cavendish, whose landscape fills her books. She trained as a teacher and worked briefly for a Halifax newspaper while writing for magazines. In 1911 she married the Reverend Ewan Macdonald and moved to Ontario, where she raised two sons. She died in Toronto in 1942 and was buried in Cavendish.

Anne of Green Gables, published in 1908, tells of Anne Shirley, a talkative, imaginative orphan sent by mistake to an elderly brother and sister who had wanted a boy. Its humour and warmth made it an instant success, and Montgomery wrote several sequels following Anne into adulthood. She also wrote the Emily of New Moon books and The Blue Castle. Her heroines' intelligence and love of nature still appeal to readers worldwide, and Green Gables in Cavendish attracts visitors from many countries.
Laozi: Very little is known about Laozi, whose name means Old Master. The historian Sima Qian, writing around 100 BC, said he was Li Er, keeper of the archives at the Zhou court, whom Confucius consulted. According to legend, as he left China heading west, a frontier guard asked him to record his wisdom, and he wrote a short book before disappearing. Many modern scholars think the text was compiled over time by several hands, and some doubt Laozi existed as an individual.

The Tao Te Ching is a short book of about eighty poetic chapters. It speaks of the Tao, or Way, the nameless source and pattern of all things. It praises simplicity, humility, flexibility and wu wei, effortless action in harmony with nature, often using images of water and the uncarved block. It became a foundation of Taoist philosophy and religion and is among the most translated books in the world.
Leo Tolstoy: Leo Tolstoy was born in 1828 at Yasnaya Polyana, his family's estate south of Moscow. Orphaned young, he studied at Kazan University but left without a degree. He served in the army in the Caucasus and in the Crimean War at Sevastopol. In 1862 he married Sophia Behrs, who bore him thirteen children. A spiritual crisis in middle age led him to a radical Christianity of non-violence and simplicity, and the Church excommunicated him. In 1910 he left home and died at a railway station at Astapovo.

War and Peace follows aristocratic families through Napoleon's invasion of Russia, combining intimate lives with sweeping history. Anna Karenina tells of a married woman's passion for an officer alongside the search for meaning of the landowner Levin. He also wrote The Death of Ivan Ilyich and Resurrection. His moral writings on non-violence influenced Gandhi, with whom he corresponded. His realism and psychological insight make him one of the greatest novelists of all time.
Lewis Carroll: Charles Lutwidge Dodgson was born in 1832 in Daresbury, Cheshire, the eldest son of a large clergyman's family. He studied at Rugby School and Christ Church, Oxford, where he lectured in mathematics for the rest of his life. He was ordained deacon and was a skilled early photographer. He befriended the dean's children, including Alice Liddell, and on a boating trip in 1862 told them the story that became his most famous book. He died in Guildford in 1898.

Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, published in 1865 under the pen name Lewis Carroll with illustrations by John Tenniel, follows Alice into a topsy-turvy world of the White Rabbit, the Mad Hatter and the Queen of Hearts. Through the Looking-Glass, which includes the nonsense poem Jabberwocky, followed in 1871. He also wrote The Hunting of the Snark and books on logic. His playful nonsense and wordplay delight children and intrigue adults, and Alice remains one of literature's most adapted characters.
Louisa May Alcott: Louisa May Alcott was born in 1832 in Germantown, Pennsylvania, the second of four daughters of the Transcendentalist educator Amos Bronson Alcott. She grew up mostly in Concord, Massachusetts, where Emerson and Thoreau were family friends. Because her father rarely earned money, she worked as a seamstress, governess, teacher and servant and wrote to support her family. During the Civil War she served as a nurse in Washington until she fell seriously ill. A supporter of abolition and women's rights, she died in Boston in 1888, two days after her father.

Alcott's Hospital Sketches drew on her nursing experience, and she also wrote sensational thrillers under a pen name. Little Women, published in 1868 and 1869, follows the four March sisters growing up during the Civil War, with the independent Jo inspired by Alcott herself. Its warmth, humour and honest picture of family life made it a lasting success. She continued the story in Little Men and Jo's Boys.
Marcus Aurelius: Marcus Aurelius was born in Rome in AD 121 into a wealthy and well-connected family. The emperor Hadrian took an interest in him and arranged his adoption by the future emperor Antoninus Pius. He received an excellent education in rhetoric and philosophy and was drawn especially to Stoicism. He became emperor in 161, at first sharing power with Lucius Verus. His reign was troubled by plague and long wars along the Danube. He died in 180 and was succeeded by his son Commodus.

The Meditations, written in Greek, were private notes never intended for publication, probably composed partly on campaign. In short reflections he urges himself to act justly, accept what lies beyond his control, remember life's brevity and treat others patiently. The book is a key source for Stoic philosophy and a rare window into the mind of a ruler trying to live well, still read for its practical wisdom.
Mark Twain: Samuel Langhorne Clemens was born in 1835 in Missouri and grew up in Hannibal, on the Mississippi River. After his father's death he was apprenticed to a printer. He became a riverboat pilot until the Civil War halted river traffic, then went west, where as a journalist he first used the pen name Mark Twain. He married Olivia Langdon and settled in Hartford, Connecticut. Bad investments led to bankruptcy, which he repaid through a world lecture tour. He died in Connecticut in 1910.

Twain became famous with comic sketches and travel books such as The Innocents Abroad. The Adventures of Tom Sawyer celebrated boyhood along the Mississippi. Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, told in Huck's own voice as he travels down the river with Jim, a man escaping slavery, is often called one of the great American novels. He also wrote A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court. His humour, satire and ear for American speech keep him widely read.
Mary Shelley: Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin was born in London in 1797, the daughter of the writer Mary Wollstonecraft, who died days after her birth, and the philosopher William Godwin. At sixteen she eloped with the poet Percy Bysshe Shelley. In the summer of 1816, near Lord Byron by Lake Geneva, a ghost-story contest gave her the idea for her first novel, and the couple married that December. Several of her children died young; in 1822 Percy drowned off Italy. Back in England, she supported herself and her son by writing. She died in London in 1851.

Frankenstein was published anonymously in 1818, when Mary was twenty. It tells of Victor Frankenstein, a young scientist who creates a living being and then abandons it, with tragic results. Exploring ambition, responsibility and loneliness, it is often seen as one of the first science fiction novels. She also wrote The Last Man, about a plague that destroys humanity. Her creature remains one of the most enduring figures of modern myth.
Miguel de Cervantes: Miguel de Cervantes was born in 1547 in Alcalá de Henares, near Madrid, the son of a surgeon. As a young soldier he fought at the battle of Lepanto in 1571, where a wound left his left hand useless. In 1575 he was captured by pirates and held in Algiers for five years before being ransomed. Back in Spain he worked as a tax collector, a job that led to imprisonment over his accounts. He died in Madrid in 1616.

After a pastoral romance, plays and poems, success came only with Don Quixote. Its first part, published in 1605, follows an elderly gentleman who reads so many chivalric romances that he sets out as a knight errant with the squire Sancho Panza; the second followed in 1615. Mixing comedy, parody and reflection on reality and imagination, it is often called the first modern novel. The word quixotic comes from his masterpiece.
Nathaniel Hawthorne: Nathaniel Hawthorne was born in 1804 in Salem, Massachusetts. One of his Puritan ancestors had been a judge at the Salem witch trials, a legacy that troubled him. His father, a sea captain, died when Nathaniel was a child. At Bowdoin College his classmates included the poet Longfellow and the future president Franklin Pierce. He spent years writing in seclusion, briefly joined the utopian community of Brook Farm, and married Sophia Peabody. He worked at the Salem Custom House and as US consul in Liverpool, and died in 1864.

His stories include Young Goodman Brown and Rappaccini's Daughter. The Scarlet Letter, published in 1850, tells of Hester Prynne, forced to wear a scarlet A for adultery in Puritan Boston, and of the hidden guilt of her lover, the minister Dimmesdale. It was followed by The House of the Seven Gables. Hawthorne explored sin, guilt and the weight of the past, and he influenced Herman Melville, who dedicated Moby-Dick to him.
Niccolò Machiavelli: Niccolò Machiavelli was born in Florence in 1469, the son of a lawyer, and received a humanist education. In 1498 he became secretary of the Florentine republic's second chancery and was sent on missions to the king of France, Cesare Borgia and the papal court. When the Medici returned in 1512 he lost his post, and the following year he was imprisoned and tortured on suspicion of conspiracy. Released, he retired to his farm outside Florence. He died in 1527.

In retirement Machiavelli wrote The Prince, a short guide for a new ruler, which circulated in manuscript and was published in 1532, after his death. It argues that a ruler must sometimes act ruthlessly, judging actions by their results rather than conventional morality. His Discourses on Livy praise republican government, and he also wrote the comedy The Mandrake. The word Machiavellian came to mean cunning, but his realistic analysis of politics made him a founder of modern political science.
Omar Khayyam: Omar Khayyam was born in 1048 in Nishapur, in the region of Khorasan in present-day Iran, during the rule of the Seljuk Turks. A leading mathematician and astronomer, he worked at an observatory in Isfahan under Sultan Malik-Shah and helped create a remarkably accurate solar calendar. His treatise on algebra solved cubic equations using geometry. He later returned to Nishapur, where he died around 1131 and where his tomb still stands.

Many short four-line poems, or rubaiyat, have been attributed to Khayyam, though scholars agree that a large number were written by others. They reflect on the brevity of life, the limits of human knowledge and the pleasures of wine, love and the present moment. In 1859 the English poet Edward FitzGerald published a free and inventive version, The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, which became hugely popular in the English-speaking world. Today Khayyam is admired both as a scientist and as a poetic voice of doubt and delight.
Oscar Wilde: Oscar Wilde was born in Dublin in 1854, the son of a celebrated surgeon and a nationalist poet. He studied classics at Trinity College Dublin and Magdalen College, Oxford, becoming a voice of aestheticism, the belief in art for art's sake. He lectured across America in 1882 and married Constance Lloyd, with whom he had two sons. In 1895, after a failed libel case against the father of his lover Lord Alfred Douglas, he was sentenced to two years' hard labour for gross indecency. He died in poverty in Paris in 1900.

Wilde wrote fairy tales such as The Happy Prince. The Picture of Dorian Gray, his only novel, tells of a young man whose portrait ages while he stays beautiful. His comedies, including An Ideal Husband and The Importance of Being Earnest, sparkle with wit while mocking Victorian society. Prison produced the long letter De Profundis and The Ballad of Reading Gaol. His epigrams are still quoted everywhere.
Ovid: Publius Ovidius Naso was born in 43 BC in Sulmo, east of Rome, into a family of the equestrian class. Educated in rhetoric at Rome, he gave up a public career for poetry and became the most fashionable poet of Augustus's Rome. In AD 8 the emperor banished him to Tomis on the Black Sea, in present-day Romania; the exact reason remains a mystery, though Ovid himself blamed a poem and an error. Never allowed to return, he died in exile around AD 17 or 18.

Ovid's early works include the Amores, love elegies, the Heroides, letters from mythical heroines to absent lovers, and the playful Art of Love. His masterpiece, the Metamorphoses, weaves together some two hundred and fifty myths of transformation, including Daphne and Apollo, Echo and Narcissus, and Pygmalion. In exile he wrote the sorrowful Tristia. His storytelling inspired Chaucer, Shakespeare and painters such as Titian, and the Metamorphoses remains a treasury of classical myth.
Plato: Plato was born in Athens around 428 BC into an aristocratic family. As a young man he followed the philosopher Socrates, whose execution in 399 BC turned him away from politics. He visited Sicily, where he tried without success to influence the ruler of Syracuse. Around 387 BC he founded the Academy in Athens, where Aristotle later studied. He taught and wrote there until his death around 348 BC.

Plato wrote dialogues, most featuring Socrates questioning others about justice, virtue, love, knowledge and the soul. The Apology, Crito and Phaedo portray Socrates' trial and death; the Symposium explores love; and the Republic describes an ideal state ruled by philosopher-kings and includes the famous allegory of the cave. Central to his thought is the theory of Forms, the idea that perfect, unchanging realities lie behind the world we perceive. His works shaped philosophy, theology and politics, making him one of the most influential thinkers in history.
Robert Louis Stevenson: Robert Louis Stevenson was born in Edinburgh in 1850 into a famous family of lighthouse engineers. A sickly child, he studied engineering and then law at Edinburgh but chose to write. Travels in France produced his first books, including Travels with a Donkey in the Cévennes. He fell in love with an American, Fanny Osbourne, followed her to California and married her in 1880. Seeking a healthier climate, he sailed the Pacific and in 1890 settled in Samoa, where he died in 1894.

Stevenson won wide fame with Treasure Island, published in 1883, the story of young Jim Hawkins and the pirate Long John Silver that defined the image of pirates for generations. Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde explores the duality of good and evil, and Kidnapped follows a young Scot after the Jacobite rising. He also wrote The Master of Ballantrae and the poems of A Child's Garden of Verses.
Rudyard Kipling: Rudyard Kipling was born in Bombay in 1865, where his father taught art. At five he was sent to a foster family in England, an unhappy experience, and later attended school in Devon. At sixteen he returned to India as a journalist in Lahore. Famous in London in his twenties, he married Caroline Balestier, lived for some years in Vermont and settled in Sussex. His son John was killed in the First World War. He received the Nobel Prize in 1907 and died in London in 1936.

His early stories, Plain Tales from the Hills, and Barrack-Room Ballads brought British India vividly to life. The Jungle Book and its sequel, with Mowgli, Baloo and Shere Khan, became children's classics, as did the Just So Stories. Kim, his finest novel, follows an orphan boy on the roads of India. His poems, including If, remain widely quoted. His support for empire makes him controversial, but his storytelling keeps him widely read.
Selma Lagerlöf: Selma Lagerlöf was born in 1858 at Mårbacka, her family's estate in the province of Värmland, Sweden. A hip problem left her with a limp, and as a child she absorbed local legends. She trained as a teacher in Stockholm and taught in Landskrona for about ten years, while the family lost Mårbacka. Success with her first novel let her write full-time and travel to Italy and the Middle East. She bought back Mårbacka in stages, completing the purchase with her Nobel Prize money, became the first woman in the Swedish Academy, and died there in 1940.

Her first novel, Gösta Berling's Saga, published in 1891, brought the folklore of Värmland to life. She went on to write Jerusalem and many other novels and stories. The Wonderful Adventures of Nils, commissioned as a school geography reader, follows a boy shrunk to tiny size who travels across Sweden on a goose. In 1909 she became the first woman to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature.
Stendhal: Marie-Henri Beyle was born in Grenoble in 1783. His mother died when he was seven, and he grew up resenting his father and his conservative home. Arriving in Paris in 1799, he followed Napoleon's army into Italy, beginning a lifelong love of the country, especially Milan. He served the imperial administration and survived the retreat from Moscow in 1812. After Napoleon's fall he lived in Milan and later served as French consul at Civitavecchia. He died in Paris in 1842.

Using the pen name Stendhal, he wrote On Love and travel books. The Red and the Black, published in 1830, follows Julien Sorel, an ambitious young man of humble birth who tries to rise in Restoration France through seduction and hypocrisy. The Charterhouse of Parma, published in 1839, follows a young Italian aristocrat and opens with a famous portrayal of Waterloo. Stendhal's sharp psychological analysis made him a pioneer of the realist novel.
Thomas Hardy: Thomas Hardy was born in 1840 at Higher Bockhampton, near Dorchester in Dorset, the son of a stonemason and builder. He trained as an architect while reading widely and writing poetry. While restoring a church in Cornwall he met Emma Gifford, whom he married in 1874. After the hostile reception of Jude the Obscure, he gave up fiction and devoted himself to poetry. Emma died in 1912; he later married Florence Dugdale and died at Max Gate, his Dorchester home, in 1928.

Hardy set his novels in Wessex, a fictional version of south-west England. Far from the Madding Crowd brought him fame in 1874, followed by The Mayor of Casterbridge, Tess of the d'Urbervilles and Jude the Obscure. His novels portray characters crushed by chance and social convention, challenging Victorian attitudes to class, marriage and religion. In later decades he wrote hundreds of poems, including moving elegies for Emma, and he is honoured as a major English poet.
Thomas Malthus: Thomas Robert Malthus was born in 1766 near Dorking, Surrey, England. He studied mathematics at Jesus College, Cambridge, and was ordained in the Church of England. In 1805 he became professor of political economy at the East India Company's college, one of the first such posts in Britain. He was a close friend and frequent intellectual opponent of David Ricardo. He died in 1834.

An Essay on the Principle of Population, first published anonymously in 1798 and greatly expanded in later editions, responded to optimists who believed society could be perfected. Malthus argued that population tends to grow faster than the food supply, so that it is held back by hunger, disease and misery unless people delay marriage and have fewer children. His Principles of Political Economy followed in 1820. His ideas fuelled debates about poverty and the poor laws, and they helped inspire Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace.
Thomas Paine: Thomas Paine was born in 1737 in Thetford, Norfolk, England, the son of a Quaker corset maker. He left school early and worked as a corset maker and excise officer. Encouraged by Benjamin Franklin, he emigrated to Philadelphia in 1774. During the Revolution he served with the army and wrote The American Crisis to sustain morale. In France he was elected to the National Convention, opposed the execution of Louis XVI, and narrowly escaped death in prison during the Terror. He returned to America in 1802 and died in New York in 1809.

Common Sense, published in January 1776, argued forcefully for American independence and helped turn opinion toward revolution. Rights of Man defended the French Revolution and called for democratic government and social welfare, leading to his prosecution in England. The Age of Reason criticised organised religion and made him many enemies. His clear, passionate prose made him one of the most influential political writers of his age.
Thorstein Veblen: Thorstein Veblen was born in 1857 in Wisconsin to Norwegian immigrant farmers and grew up in Minnesota. He earned a doctorate in philosophy at Yale but struggled to find academic work. He then taught economics at Chicago, where he edited the Journal of Political Economy, and later at Stanford, Missouri and the New School. He died in California in 1929, shortly before the stock market crash.

The Theory of the Leisure Class, published in 1899, examined how the wealthy display their status through conspicuous consumption and conspicuous leisure, and how others try to imitate them. In The Theory of Business Enterprise and later books, Veblen contrasted the productive work of engineers and craftsmen with the profit-seeking of business and finance. He brought ideas from anthropology and evolution into economics and is regarded as a founder of institutional economics. His analysis of status and spending still feels relevant, and luxury goods whose demand rises with price are called Veblen goods.
Victor Hugo: Victor Hugo was born in Besançon in 1802, the son of an officer in Napoleon's army. He won early fame as a poet, and his play Hernani in 1830 marked the triumph of Romanticism in French theatre. The drowning of his daughter Léopoldine in 1843 devastated him. He opposed Napoleon III's seizure of power in 1851 and spent nearly twenty years in exile, mostly on Guernsey. He returned in 1870 and, when he died in Paris in 1885, was buried in the Panthéon.

Hugo's novel The Hunchback of Notre-Dame, published in 1831, tells of Quasimodo and Esmeralda in medieval Paris and helped inspire the restoration of the cathedral. Les Misérables, completed in exile and published in 1862, follows the former convict Jean Valjean through decades of French history, pleading for justice, mercy and the poor. He also wrote poetry, plays and further novels, and campaigned against the death penalty. He is regarded as one of France's greatest writers.
