Virginia Woolf: Adeline Virginia Stephen was born in London in 1882, the daughter of the critic Sir Leslie Stephen. Denied the university education given to her brothers, she educated herself in her father's library. The deaths of her mother, half-sister, father and brother brought grief and breakdowns. Her Bloomsbury home with her siblings became a centre of the Bloomsbury Group. In 1912 she married Leonard Woolf, and together they founded the Hogarth Press. Suffering another severe depression, she drowned herself in the River Ouse in Sussex in 1941.

Mrs Dalloway, following a London hostess through a single June day, and To the Lighthouse use stream of consciousness to capture the flow of thought. Orlando follows a hero who lives for centuries and changes sex. In the essay A Room of One's Own she argued that a woman needs money and a room of her own to write. Her innovations and feminist thought make her one of the central modernist writers.
Voltaire: François-Marie Arouet was born in Paris in 1694, the son of a notary, and educated by the Jesuits. His satirical verses earned him nearly a year in the Bastille, after which he adopted the name Voltaire. After a quarrel with a nobleman he went to England, admiring its freedom and tolerance. He later lived at Cirey with the scientist Émilie du Châtelet and at the court of Frederick the Great. From 1759 he lived at Ferney, near Geneva, and he died in Paris in 1778 after a triumphant return.

Voltaire wrote plays, poems, histories, essays and more than twenty thousand letters. His Philosophical Letters praised English institutions and criticised French ones. His philosophical tales include Zadig and especially Candide, published in 1759, a brisk satire of naive optimism that ends with the advice to cultivate one's garden. He campaigned against intolerance, notably in the case of Jean Calas, and wrote the Philosophical Dictionary. He embodies the spirit of the Enlightenment.
William Makepeace Thackeray: William Makepeace Thackeray was born in Calcutta in 1811, where his father worked for the East India Company. Sent to England as a child, he attended Charterhouse and Trinity College, Cambridge, which he left without a degree. Having lost much of his inheritance, he studied art in Paris and turned to journalism, writing under comic pseudonyms for Fraser's and Punch. His wife became mentally ill a few years after their marriage. He later edited the Cornhill Magazine and died in London in 1863.

The Luck of Barry Lyndon, a picaresque tale of an Irish adventurer, was later filmed by Stanley Kubrick. His masterpiece, Vanity Fair, published in 1847 and 1848, follows the clever, unscrupulous Becky Sharp and gentle Amelia Sedley through society and the Napoleonic Wars. He also wrote Pendennis, Henry Esmond and The Newcomes, often illustrating his own work. His ironic narrator and satire of greed and social climbing made him, with Dickens, one of the leading Victorian novelists.
William Shakespeare: William Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon and baptised on 26 April 1564. His father was a glover and town official. At eighteen he married Anne Hathaway, and they had three children, including twins, Hamnet and Judith; Hamnet died at eleven. By the early 1590s Shakespeare was working in London as an actor and playwright. He became a shareholder in the Lord Chamberlain's Men, later the King's Men, and in the Globe Theatre. He later returned to Stratford, where he died in 1616.

Shakespeare wrote around thirty-seven plays, some in collaboration, as well as 154 sonnets and long narrative poems. They include comedies such as Twelfth Night, tragedies including Romeo and Juliet, Hamlet, Othello, King Lear and Macbeth, and late romances such as The Tempest. In 1623 two fellow actors collected his plays in the First Folio. His insight into human nature and inventive language make his works the most performed and studied in the world.
Émile Zola: Émile Zola was born in Paris in 1840. His Italian-born father died when Émile was a child, and he grew up poor in Aix-en-Provence, befriending Paul Cézanne. Back in Paris, he worked for the publisher Hachette while writing journalism and art criticism defending Manet. In 1898, during the Dreyfus Affair, he was convicted of libel for defending the wrongly condemned officer and fled to England. He died in Paris in 1902 of carbon monoxide poisoning from a blocked chimney.

Zola's early novel Thérèse Raquin was followed by his great cycle, Les Rougon-Macquart, twenty novels tracing one family's branches under the Second Empire. It includes L'Assommoir, about alcoholism among Paris workers, Nana, The Ladies' Paradise, Germinal, about a miners' strike, and La Bête humaine. As the leading voice of naturalism, he aimed to study human behaviour shaped by heredity and environment with scientific rigour. His open letter J'accuse...!, published in 1898, became a landmark of political courage.
Ann Radcliffe: Ann Radcliffe was born Ann Ward in London in 1764, the only child of a haberdasher. Little is known about her early life. In 1787 she married William Radcliffe, a graduate of Oxford who became the owner and editor of the English Chronicle newspaper, and she began writing novels soon afterwards. Shy and private, she avoided literary society, which led to many false rumours about her during her lifetime. She died in London in 1823.

Her first novels, The Castles of Athlin and Dunbayne (1789), A Sicilian Romance (1790) and The Romance of the Forest (1791), established her style. The Mysteries of Udolpho (1794) made her the best-known and best-paid novelist of the 1790s, and The Italian (1797) confirmed her reputation. She then stopped publishing novels. Her blend of sublime landscapes, suspense and rationally explained terrors shaped the Gothic novel and influenced Scott, Byron, Mary Shelley and Poe.
Wilkie Collins: William Wilkie Collins was born in London in 1824, the son of the landscape painter William Collins. He spent part of his childhood in Italy and France, worked for a tea merchant, then studied law and was called to the bar in 1851, though he never practised. That same year he met Charles Dickens, who became his close friend, editor and occasional collaborator. Collins lived an unconventional private life, sharing his home with Caroline Graves while also having a second family with Martha Rudd. He suffered from painful illness for many years, took large doses of laudanum, and died in London in 1889.

Collins became famous with The Woman in White (1859-1860), serialised in Dickens's magazine All the Year Round, which helped create the 'sensation novel' of the 1860s. It was followed by No Name, Armadale and The Moonstone (1868), often called the first great English detective novel. His gift for suspense, complex plots told by several narrators, and interest in social injustice made him one of the most popular writers of his time and a major influence on mystery fiction.
Walter Scott: Walter Scott was born in Edinburgh on 15 August 1771. An attack of polio in early childhood left him lame for life, and he spent part of his childhood on his grandparents' farm in the Scottish Borders, where he heard the ballads and legends that would feed his work. He studied law, became an advocate in 1792 and was appointed Sheriff of Selkirkshire in 1799. In 1811 he bought a farm on the River Tweed which he rebuilt as his home, Abbotsford, and in 1820 he was made a baronet. The collapse of the Ballantyne printing business, in which he was a partner, left him with enormous debts in 1826; refusing bankruptcy, he worked tirelessly to repay them until his death at Abbotsford on 21 September 1832.

Scott first became famous as a poet and collector of ballads, with Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border (1802–1803), The Lay of the Last Minstrel (1805), Marmion (1808) and The Lady of the Lake (1810). In 1814 he published Waverley anonymously, the first of a long series of novels including Rob Roy (1817), The Heart of Mid-Lothian (1818), Ivanhoe (1819), Kenilworth (1821) and Quentin Durward (1823); he only acknowledged his authorship after his financial ruin. Combining vivid history, adventure and regional character, the Waverley novels were read all over Europe and America and inspired writers such as Balzac, Victor Hugo, Alessandro Manzoni and James Fenimore Cooper.
Friedrich Nietzsche: Friedrich Wilhelm Nietzsche was born on 15 October 1844 in Röcken, in Prussian Saxony, the son of a Lutheran pastor. He studied at the famous boarding school of Schulpforta and then classical philology at the universities of Bonn and Leipzig, and in 1869, at only 24, he was appointed professor at the University of Basel in Switzerland. There he became a close friend of Richard Wagner, before breaking with him. Constant ill health forced him to resign in 1879, and he spent the following decade travelling between Switzerland, Italy and the south of France, writing his major books. In January 1889 he suffered a mental collapse in Turin from which he never recovered; he was cared for by his mother and then his sister, and died in Weimar on 25 August 1900.

His works include The Birth of Tragedy (1872), Human, All Too Human (1878), The Gay Science (1882), Thus Spake Zarathustra (1883–1885), Beyond Good and Evil (1886), On the Genealogy of Morality (1887), Twilight of the Idols and The Antichrist (1888). After his death his sister, Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche, took control of his manuscripts and edited them to suit her nationalist views, which encouraged the later misuse of his ideas by the Nazis; twentieth-century scholars restored his texts. His critique of morality, religion and truth deeply influenced modern philosophy, literature and psychology.
Elizabeth Gaskell: Elizabeth Cleghorn Stevenson was born on 29 September 1810 in Chelsea, London. Her mother died when she was a baby, and she was brought up by an aunt in Knutsford, Cheshire, a small town that later inspired her fiction. In 1832 she married William Gaskell, a Unitarian minister at Cross Street Chapel in Manchester, where the couple lived and raised their family. After the death of their infant son, she turned to writing. She died suddenly on 12 November 1865 at Holybourne in Hampshire, aged 55.

Her first novel, Mary Barton (1848), described the lives of the Manchester poor and made her name. It was followed by Cranford and Ruth (both 1853), North and South (1855), the pioneering biography The Life of Charlotte Brontë (1857), Sylvia's Lovers (1863) and Wives and Daughters, left unfinished at her death and published in 1866. Cranford and North and South first appeared in Household Words, the magazine edited by Charles Dickens.
Anne Brontë: Anne Brontë was born on 17 January 1820 at Thornton, Yorkshire, the youngest of the six children of the Reverend Patrick Brontë and his wife Maria Branwell, and grew up at Haworth with her sisters Charlotte and Emily and her brother Branwell. She worked as a governess for several years, including from 1840 at Thorp Green, a country house near York, in the family of the Reverend Edmund Robinson. She died, probably of tuberculosis, at Scarborough on 28 May 1849, aged 29.

Writing as Acton Bell, she published poems with her sisters in 1846, then Agnes Grey in 1847, based on her experience as a governess. Her second and last novel, The Tenant of Wildfell Hall (1848), a bold story of a woman leaving an abusive marriage, is often described as one of the first feminist novels.
Horace Walpole: Horatio Walpole, known as Horace, was born in London on 24 September 1717, the youngest son of the Prime Minister Sir Robert Walpole. He became a Whig member of Parliament, an art historian and an antiquarian, and late in life succeeded as 4th Earl of Orford. At Twickenham, near London, he built Strawberry Hill, a house that revived the Gothic style decades before the Victorians. He died on 2 March 1797.

Walpole is remembered above all for The Castle of Otranto (1764), generally regarded as the first Gothic novel, and for his letters. More than 3,000 of them survive, covering the years 1732 to 1797, and they give a lively and detailed picture of Georgian England.
Oliver Goldsmith: Oliver Goldsmith was born in Ireland on 10 November, in 1728 according to most sources and 1730 according to others, the son of a clergyman. He studied at Trinity College Dublin, travelled in Europe, and settled in London, where he made a living as a hack writer, translator and journalist. In 1764 he became one of the first members of Samuel Johnson's literary circle, known as The Club. He died in London on 4 April 1774.

Goldsmith wrote in many forms: the novel The Vicar of Wakefield (1766), the long poem The Deserted Village (1770), and the comedy She Stoops to Conquer (1773), still performed today, as well as essays, histories and works of popular science.
Frances Burney: Frances Burney, known as Fanny, was born on 13 June 1752 in King's Lynn, Norfolk. From 1786 she served at the court of Queen Charlotte as Keeper of the Robes, and her diaries and letters from those years give a detailed picture of court life, including the illness of King George III. In 1793 she married a French exile, General Alexandre d'Arblay. She died on 6 January 1840.

After the success of Evelina (1778) she published Cecilia (1782), Camilla (1796) and The Wanderer (1814), novels about the lives of young women in society. Her journals and letters are also celebrated, among them her account of a mastectomy she underwent without anaesthetic in Paris, one of the earliest and most detailed descriptions of such an operation.
Edward Bulwer-Lytton: Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer-Lytton was born in London on 25 May 1803. Besides writing, he had a long political career and served as Secretary of State for the Colonies from June 1858 to June 1859. He was later raised to the peerage as Baron Lytton. He died in Torquay on 18 January 1873.

A prolific and widely read author, he began with the novel Pelham (1828) and wrote historical, social and occult fiction, plays and poetry. He coined phrases that are still in use, such as "the pen is mightier than the sword", and the opening "It was a dark and stormy night".
R. D. Blackmore: Richard Doddridge Blackmore was born on 7 June 1825 at Longworth, Berkshire. He studied at Exeter College, Oxford, and trained as a barrister, but owing to poor health he gave up the law and turned to market-gardening and writing at Teddington, Middlesex, where he grew fruit and rare plants. He died at Teddington on 20 January 1900.

Blackmore wrote poetry, translations and several other novels, and was among the best-known English novelists of the second half of the nineteenth century. Today he is remembered almost entirely for Lorna Doone, which has remained continuously popular.
Anthony Trollope: Anthony Trollope was born in London on 24 April 1815. His family was often in financial difficulty, and his mother, Frances Trollope, began a successful writing career to support it. He worked for the Post Office from 1834 to 1867, and from 1841 he spent many years in Ireland as a postal official. He died in London on 6 December 1882.

Trollope wrote 47 novels, famously working early in the morning at a fixed pace. His best-known works are two series of six novels each, the Chronicles of Barsetshire, including Barchester Towers (1857), and the Palliser novels. He also wrote travel books, short stories and an autobiography.
Henry James: Henry James was born in New York City on 15 April 1843 and spent much of his youth travelling in Europe. He settled in England and became a British citizen in 1915, as a sign of loyalty to his adopted country during the First World War. He died in London on 28 February 1916.

James is known for subtle psychological novels and stories, often about Americans in Europe, such as Daisy Miller (1879), The Portrait of a Lady (1881) and The Ambassadors (1903). He also wrote ghost stories, criticism and travel writing, and is considered one of the great masters of the novel.
Kate Chopin: Kate Chopin was born Katherine O'Flaherty in St. Louis, Missouri, on 8 February 1850. In 1870 she married Oscar Chopin, the son of a Louisiana Creole family, and lived in New Orleans and later in Cloutierville, Louisiana, raising six children. After her husband's death in 1882 she began to write. She died on 22 August 1904.

Chopin wrote around a hundred short stories, many set among the Creole and Cajun people of Louisiana, collected in volumes such as Bayou Folk, and two novels, of which The Awakening (1899) is the best known. Neglected for decades after her death, she is now regarded as an important early feminist writer.
Stephen Crane: Stephen Crane was born on 1 November 1871 in Newark, New Jersey, the fourteenth and last child of a Methodist minister. He worked as a journalist in New York and later as a war correspondent, including in Cuba during the Spanish–American War. Suffering from tuberculosis, he died at Badenweiler in Germany on 5 June 1900, aged 28.

His first book, Maggie: A Girl of the Streets (1893), which he published himself under a pseudonym, is often considered a founding work of American literary naturalism. The Red Badge of Courage (1895) made him famous. He also wrote poetry and short stories, among them "The Open Boat" (1898), based on his own experience of a shipwreck.
Willa Cather: Willa Cather was born on 7 December 1873 near Winchester, Virginia. When she was nine her family moved to Nebraska, and she grew up in the small prairie town of Red Cloud, which inspired much of her fiction. After working as a journalist and teacher, she became managing editor of McClure's Magazine in New York, leaving in 1912 to devote herself to writing. She died in New York City on 24 April 1947.
Her best-known novels include O Pioneers! (1913), My Ántonia (1918) and Death Comes for the Archbishop (1927). She won the Pulitzer Prize in 1923 for One of Ours (1922).
Sinclair Lewis: Sinclair Lewis was born on 7 February 1885 in Sauk Centre, Minnesota, the son of a doctor. He studied at Yale, leaving for a time to live in Upton Sinclair's socialist colony before graduating in 1908, and worked as a journalist and editor before his success as a novelist. He died near Rome on 10 January 1951.

His best-known novels, Main Street (1920), Babbitt (1922), Arrowsmith (1925), Elmer Gantry (1927), Dodsworth (1929) and It Can't Happen Here (1935), satirise American society. He declined the Pulitzer Prize awarded to Arrowsmith, and in 1930 became the first American to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
Anna Sewell: Anna Sewell was born on 30 March 1820 in Great Yarmouth, Norfolk, into a Quaker family; her mother, Mary Sewell, also became a writer. In 1832, at the age of twelve, she fell on her way home from school and injured her ankles, and for the rest of her life she walked with crutches. She died on 25 April 1878.

Sewell wrote Black Beauty during the last years of her life at Old Catton, near Norwich, while in poor health. Published in 1877, only five months before her death, it was her only book, and it has remained a classic of children's literature and of animal welfare.
Theodore Dreiser: Theodore Dreiser was born in Terre Haute, Indiana, on 27 August 1871, into a large and poor family. He worked for about ten years as a journalist, writing about life in fast-growing cities such as Chicago and New York, before turning to fiction. He died in Hollywood, California, on 28 December 1945.

Dreiser was the leading American writer of the naturalist school, showing how money, environment and social pressures shape people's lives. His best-known novels are Sister Carrie (1900) and An American Tragedy (1925).
Lew Wallace: Lew Wallace was born on 10 April 1827 in Brookville, Indiana. He served in the Mexican War and in the American Civil War, in which he rose to the rank of major general. He was later governor of the New Mexico Territory from 1878 to 1881 and United States minister to the Ottoman Empire from 1881 to 1885. He died in Crawfordsville, Indiana, on 15 February 1905.

Wallace wrote Ben-Hur (1880) while governor of New Mexico. Its enormous success made it one of the most influential Christian books of the nineteenth century, and it remains by far his best-known work.
Eleanor H. Porter: Eleanor Emily Hodgman Porter was born on 19 December 1868 in Littleton, New Hampshire. She published stories in magazines and a number of novels for adults and young readers. She died on 21 May 1920.
Her best-known book by far is Pollyanna (1913), a classic of children's literature, followed by its sequel Pollyanna Grows Up (1915).
Charlotte Perkins Gilman: Charlotte Perkins Gilman was born in Hartford, Connecticut, on 3 July 1860. She became a leading writer, lecturer and theorist of the women's movement, arguing that women's economic independence was essential to the progress of society. From 1909 to 1916 she wrote and edited her own magazine, The Forerunner. She died in Pasadena, California, on 17 August 1935.

She is best known for the short story "The Yellow Wall-Paper" (1892) and the study Women and Economics (1898). Her many other works include novels such as Herland (1915), short stories, poems and thousands of essays.
Kate Douglas Wiggin: Kate Douglas Wiggin was born in Philadelphia on 28 September 1856. In 1878 she opened the first free kindergarten in San Francisco, the Silver Street Free Kindergarten, and she became a leader of the kindergarten movement in the United States. She died on 24 August 1923 at Harrow, in England.
Alongside her work in education she wrote many stories and novels for children and adults, of which Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm (1903) is the best known.
H. Rider Haggard: Henry Rider Haggard was born on 22 June 1856 at Bradenham, Norfolk. As a young man he served in colonial administration in South Africa, in Natal and later in the Transvaal, experiences that shaped his fiction. Back in England he became known both as a writer and for his work on agriculture and rural reform. He was knighted, and died in London on 14 May 1925.
Haggard wrote more than thirty adventure novels, many set in Africa. The most famous are King Solomon's Mines (1885) and She (1887), which made him one of the best-selling authors of his day.
George Bernard Shaw: George Bernard Shaw was born in Dublin on 26 July 1856 and moved to London as a young man. A committed socialist, he was a member of the Fabian Society. He died on 2 November 1950.

Shaw wrote more than sixty plays, including Arms and the Man, Mrs Warren's Profession, Major Barbara and Pygmalion. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1925 and an Academy Award for the screenplay of the 1938 film of Pygmalion.
Henrik Ibsen: Henrik Ibsen was born on 20 March 1828 in Skien, Norway. After his father's business failed, he worked as an apothecary's apprentice before becoming a theatre director and resident playwright in Bergen. In 1864 he left Norway and lived for many years in Italy and Germany, returning home in 1891. He died in Kristiania, now Oslo, on 23 May 1906.

His works include the verse dramas Brand (1865) and Peer Gynt (1867) and the realistic plays A Doll's House (1879), Ghosts (1881), An Enemy of the People (1882), The Wild Duck (1884) and Hedda Gabler (1890), which transformed European theatre.
Anthony Hope: Sir Anthony Hope Hawkins, who wrote as Anthony Hope, was born in London on 9 February 1863. He was educated at Marlborough College and Balliol College, Oxford, and became a lawyer, writing short stories in his spare time before the success of his novels allowed him to write full-time. He died on 8 July 1933.
Although he wrote many novels and plays, he is remembered above all for The Prisoner of Zenda (1894) and its sequel Rupert of Hentzau (1898), set in the imaginary kingdom of Ruritania.
Prosper Mérimée: Prosper Mérimée was born in Paris on 28 September 1803. For many years he served as inspector-general of historical monuments, protecting and restoring many great buildings of France, including the walled city of Carcassonne. He was elected to the Académie française in 1844 and became a senator under the Second Empire. He died in Cannes on 23 September 1870.
A master of the short novel, he wrote Mateo Falcone (1829), Colomba (1840) and Carmen (1845), among other works. He also learned Russian and translated writers such as Pushkin and Gogol into French.
Molière: Molière was the stage name of Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, baptised in Paris on 15 January 1622, the eldest son of a prosperous family of upholsterers. He gave up the family business for the theatre and became the leading comic playwright of his day. He died in Paris on 17 February 1673, shortly after performing in his last play, The Imaginary Invalid.

His comedies, including The School for Wives, Tartuffe, Don Juan, The Misanthrope, The Miser and The Imaginary Invalid, satirise hypocrisy, pretension and folly, and are among the greatest works of French literature.
Ivan Turgenev: Ivan Turgenev was born on 9 November 1818 in Oryol, Russia, into a rich landowning family, and studied in Moscow and St Petersburg. A lifelong attachment to the famous singer Pauline Viardot shaped his life, and he spent his later years mostly abroad, in Baden-Baden and Paris. He died at Bougival, near Paris, on 3 September 1883.
His first major work, A Sportsman's Sketches (1852), was a milestone of Russian realism. His novels include Fathers and Sons (1862), his most famous work, and Smoke.
Abbé Prévost: Antoine François Prévost d'Exiles, known as the Abbé Prévost, was born at Hesdin, in northern France, on 1 April 1697. He was a priest, novelist, journalist and translator, and led an adventurous life. He died on 25 November 1763.
His best-known work is the seven-volume Memoirs and Adventures of a Man of Quality (1728–1731), whose final volume is Manon Lescaut.
Nikolai Gogol: Nikolai Gogol was born in 1809 in Sorochintsy, near Poltava, in Ukraine, then part of the Russian Empire. His Ukrainian stories, Evenings on a Farm near Dikanka (1831), quickly made him famous. After his comedy The Government Inspector was attacked in 1836, he lived abroad for most of the next twelve years. He died in Moscow on 4 March 1852.

Gogol blended fantasy, satire and realism in a way that deeply influenced Russian literature. Besides Taras Bulba, his best-known works include the play The Government Inspector (1836), the stories of St Petersburg such as "The Overcoat", and the novel Dead Souls, whose first part appeared in 1842.
George Sand: George Sand was the pen name of Amantine Lucile Aurore Dupin, born in Paris on 1 July 1804. She spent much of her life at Nohant, in the Berry region of central France, which inspired many of her novels, and became one of the most famous and independent women of her century. She died at Nohant on 8 June 1876.

One of the most widely read writers of her time, she published dozens of novels as well as plays and essays. Her first novel, Indiana (1832), defended a woman's right to follow her heart, and her rustic novels such as La Mare au Diable (1846) celebrated rural life.
Marcel Proust: Marcel Proust was born on 10 July 1871 in Auteuil, then on the edge of Paris. He suffered from asthma from the age of nine, and his poor health made him increasingly reclusive; in his later years he wrote mainly at night in his cork-lined bedroom in Paris. He died on 18 November 1922.

His life's work is the vast novel In Search of Lost Time (À la recherche du temps perdu), published in seven volumes from 1913 onwards, the last of them after his death. Its second volume, In the Shadow of Young Girls in Flower, won the Prix Goncourt in 1919 and made him famous.
Madame de La Fayette: Marie-Madeleine Pioche de La Vergne, later Comtesse de La Fayette, was born in Paris in March 1634. A cultivated woman who moved in the circles of the court and the literary salons, she died in Paris in May 1693.
Her masterpiece, The Princess of Clèves (1678), was published anonymously and is often regarded as the first great French novel.
François-René de Chateaubriand: François-René de Chateaubriand was born at Saint-Malo, in Brittany, on 4 September 1768, into an old aristocratic family. He lived in exile in England during the French Revolution. A royalist, he later had a long political and diplomatic career. He died in Paris on 4 July 1848.

His works include Atala (1801), René and The Genius of Christianity (1802), a defence of the Catholic faith, and his great autobiography, Memoirs from Beyond the Grave, published after his death. His work deeply influenced French literature of the nineteenth century.
Richard Brinsley Sheridan: Richard Brinsley Sheridan was born on 30 October 1751. Irish by birth, he made his name in London as a playwright and became the long-term owner of the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane. For more than thirty years he was a Whig member of the House of Commons. He died on 7 July 1816.
His best-known plays are the comedies of manners The Rivals (1775) and The School for Scandal (1777), still performed today for their wit and comic characters.
John Buchan: John Buchan was born in Perth, Scotland, on 26 August 1875. Besides writing, he had a long public career. Raised to the peerage as Lord Tweedsmuir, he served as Governor General of Canada from 1935 until his death in Montreal on 11 February 1940.

He wrote many novels, histories and biographies. His best-known books are the adventure novels featuring Richard Hannay, beginning with The Thirty-Nine Steps (1915). In Canada he founded the Governor General's Literary Awards.
George MacDonald: George MacDonald was born on 10 December 1824 at Huntly, Aberdeenshire, in Scotland. He became a minister, writer and lecturer. He died on 18 September 1905.

He wrote novels of Scottish life, poetry, sermons and, above all, fantasy works for adults and children, such as At the Back of the North Wind and The Princess and the Goblin. He was a pioneer of fantasy literature and influenced later writers including Lewis Carroll, J. R. R. Tolkien and C. S. Lewis.
Maxim Gorky: Alexei Maximovich Peshkov was born on 28 March 1868 in Nizhny Novgorod. His father died when he was a small child, and he was brought up by his grandparents; he left school young to work and later wandered through Russia. He wrote under the pen name Maxim Gorky, "gorky" meaning "bitter" in Russian. He died on 18 June 1936.

His play The Lower Depths (1902) portrays the outcasts of Russian society. His novels include Mother (1906), and his autobiographical trilogy comprises My Childhood (1913–14), In the World (1915–16) and My Universities (1923).
Anton Chekhov: Anton Pavlovich Chekhov was born on 29 January 1860 in Taganrog, in southern Russia. He studied medicine in Moscow, graduating in 1884, while supporting his family by writing comic sketches for magazines, and he continued to practise as a doctor. Suffering from tuberculosis, he spent much of his last years in Yalta, in the Crimea. He died of the disease in July 1904 at the German spa town of Badenweiler, aged 44.
He wrote hundreds of stories, from comic sketches to longer tales such as The Lady with the Dog. His plays include Uncle Vanya (1897), Three Sisters (1901) and The Cherry Orchard (1904).
